body:
It seems you're using regex to get all the values wrapped in double quotes? This likely won't work since the parser parses out a single parameter value from the line

e.g.

This is parsed as `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo"}`
```
PARAMETER stop "foo" "bar" "baz"
```

While this is parsed as `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo bar baz"}`
```
PARAMETER stop foo "bar baz"
```

Clearly this is the wrong behaviour but implementing a parser that can handle this correctly is not worthwhile right now. 

What I have in mind is something like this to create `parameters[stop]=[]string{"foo", "bar baz"}`

```
PARAMETER stop foo
PARAMETER stop "bar baz"
```

This won't work immediately either since values are inserted into a `map[string]string` so the last value will override all previous values

body:
First of all thanks for your effort here, I can see from PR #7097 that you do polished work on the OS X side of things.
That PR should be merged as it's a good platform-specific change on a platform specific installer. 

Now this PR is a bit different as it has a very "Mac User" wording and orientation; what do I mean? Well take a look at this from your change:

```
...prompt you for administrative access in order to install
the command line executable, which in practice means symlinking 
`/Applications/Ollama.app/Contents/Resources/ollama`...
```
^^^^^^^ <- See that `Applications/Ollama/Contents`, these are all Mac OSX concerns, not linux at all, and certainly not windows, the point is, if you're going to do this, then "Do it well", Do it for all three platforms in a nice bulleted or sectioned style.

1.) The Mac OSX install is a zip that opens into an app, that when executed asks to move itself into the Applications folder, and then tells the user what it's doing and then tells the user what command to run in the terminal. It's the "Tesla Autopilot" version of all the Ollama installs.

2.) Windows is similar, you are guided through it step by step, but windows command line stuff is inherently harder due to the ambiguity of powershell vs WSL terminal and because WSL can access windows filesystem and do stuff so people often just use WSL to do terminal things. See what I mean? It's more complicated on windows.

3.) Now the linux install is fairly straightforward, but no GUI popups flash in front of the user, guiding them step-by-step on how to use Ollama. It could use some sprucing up, like "Hey here is where the models are kept, here is the file linking those weird sha looking files to the actual model names, etc" We don't have to tell them (though it's an excellent idea) where the systemctl ollama.service file is, but if we did and showed them how to add/remove environment variable lines and change startup options for ollama, that would actually be super helpful.

Now if you took the installation section and subdivided it into each of those 3 platforms, and then did a fairly decent job on each one, that would actually be awesome work and we could iterate on that and polish it.

If not, then it's better not to selectively document a single platform while neglecting the others. I can see how the reviewer would suggest that this type of platform specific documentation be located in a "getting started" style documentation guide, that would move it out of the main readme.md and let the technical writer develop the install docs without having to worry about keeping readme.md tidy, they could then go 100% and really document the install for all three platforms.

So yeah, makes alot of sense to do that, and cover all three platforms while doing so.

I've seen some issues here with concurrent downloads. 
1) Downloading from multiple clients which cancel and resume may result in an incorrect check-sum.

```
./ollama pull falcon
pulling manifest
pulling 3230a638a2da... 100% |███████| (4.2/4.2 GB, 70 MB/s)
pulling d5311aab7c4c...   0% |                     | ( 0/ 0 B) [0s:0s]
```

body:
Building these separate runners is showing the limits of how we use `go generate`. There ends up being a lot of layers of indirection, `go generate -> go logic -> build and run shell commands from go`. Let's take this opportunity to simplify and move this logic to a shell script, I whipped this up based on your logic in here:
```
#!/bin/sh

# Set ROCM path from environment variable or default to /opt/rocm
ROCM_PATH="${ROCM_PATH:-/opt/rocm}"

# Check for CUDA and generate for GGUF and GGML
if nvcc &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Building with CUDA"

    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

    cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on
    cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release

# Check for ROCM and generate for GGUF
elif [ -d "$ROCM_PATH" ]; then
    echo "Building with ROCM"

    # GGML does not support ROCM, only generate GGUF
    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_HIPBLAS=on -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$ROCM_PATH/llvm/bin/clang -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$ROCM_PATH/llvm/bin/clang++
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

# Check for OpenCL and generate for GGUF and GGML
elif clinfo &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Building with OpenCL"

    cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CLBLAST=on
    cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release

    cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_CLBLAST=on
    cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release

else
    echo "No GPU found, skipping GPU build"
fi
```

The in the `generate_linux.go` we can just call this shell script for now and keep the cuda building logic in the shell script:
```

 //go:generate cmake -S gguf -B gguf/build/cpu -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on
 //go:generate cmake --build gguf/build/cpu --target server --config Release
 
-//go:generate cmake -S ggml -B ggml/build/cuda -DLLAMA_CUBLAS=on -DLLAMA_ACCELERATE=on -DLLAMA_K_QUANTS=on
-//go:generate cmake --build ggml/build/cuda --target server --config Release

-//go:generate cmake --build gguf/build/cuda --target server --config Release
```

body:
The problem this is aiming to solve is dll dependencies.  I wanted to try to keep the main ollama.exe dependent on almost nothing so it would run without any special path setup.  Even the CPU-based llama.cpp has a hand-full of DLLs that need to get loaded, and if they aren't in the path, and we link the way we were at Go compile time, then the resulting ollama.exe would simply fail to start without any useful error message.

This allows me to augment the PATH at runtime while loading these libraries so the user doesn't have to deal with the complexities of finding the dependencies.  Instead, we can carry them as payloads and store them in the temp dir.

routes.go seems to call the initializer for llm.go (llm.Init()), which calls payload_common.go, and has it looking up which libraries are present on the host system. Based on that, it requests the necessary llama.cpp server bundles, then unpackages the libraries included in the server bundle into the /tmp/ollama######## folder it creates, and prints which libraries were loaded.

routes.go

llm.go

body:
Tegra has a caching system it uses that eats up "available memory" but is ready to be freed on demand. When I left in the 1024MB overhead, it would frequently give "falling back to CPU -> OOM" even though JTOP was showing enough memory free. I tried to find an automated system to properly report available memory to include freeable cache and the gist is that "free -m" produces the most accurate (and accurate is almost an incorrect word) depiction of free memory in Linux and should be what is used. There isn't a library or API to query the same data other than reading it directly from /proc (and in fact, that's what the `free` binary does). 

TL;DR I let the Tegra OS manage overhead as it seems to be better at it than me. Also the reported memory from the sysinfo library, the cuda driver free memory reported, and jtop were all inconsistent in the values reported.
